q: A shelter veterinarian in Texas identifies a dog with clinical signs highly suspicious for foreign animal disease (FMD). There are no laboratory results yet. What is the correct reporting action?
o: Immediately contact the state veterinarian and USDA APHIS Veterinary Services; clinical suspicion alone is sufficient for immediate FAD reporting
Wait for laboratory confirmation before reporting; a clinical diagnosis alone is insufficient
Report to the CDC because FMD is a human health emergency
Report to the local animal control authority and have the animal quarantined pending lab results
e: For foreign animal diseases (FMD, HPAI, Newcastle disease, etc.) and other highly dangerous conditions, clinical suspicion alone is the reporting trigger — you do not wait for laboratory confirmation. USDA APHIS Veterinary Services is the federal contact; the state veterinarian is the state contact. CDC is not the primary agency for animal disease reporting.

q: Which federal agency maintains the National Notifiable Disease Surveillance System (NNDSS) for human diseases in the US?
o: FDA
USDA APHIS
CDC
WOAH (formerly OIE)
e: The CDC maintains the NNDSS, which receives reports of nationally notifiable human diseases from state health departments. USDA APHIS manages animal disease reporting (including the NLRAD). WOAH is the international body for animal disease reporting between countries. FDA does not manage disease surveillance.

q: A disease is reportable in California but not in Colorado. This illustrates which feature of the US disease reporting system?
o: The CDC can override state reporting decisions for nationally notifiable diseases
The NLRAD (National List of Reportable Animal Diseases) is the sole arbiter of which diseases must be reported
Each state maintains its own list of reportable diseases; state lists vary and a disease may be reportable in some states but not others
Diseases are only reportable if they are WOAH-listed
e: State law governs reportable disease lists for both human and animal diseases within a state. There is no single federal list that overrides state authority (the NLRAD covers federally reportable conditions but states can add diseases). A disease may therefore be reportable in one state and not another.

q: Which of the following statements about Brucella canis infection in shelter dogs is most accurate?
o: B. canis infection is detectable only by blood culture; serologic screening is not useful
B. canis poses no meaningful zoonotic risk to shelter staff
Prolonged combination antibiotic therapy reliably cures B. canis infection in dogs
B. canis cannot be reliably eliminated with antibiotics; positive dogs generally cannot be considered cured and pose ongoing public health risk
e: Unlike some bacterial infections, B. canis infection in dogs cannot be reliably cured with antibiotic therapy — recurrence is common and serology may remain positive. Positive dogs present a public health risk (especially to immunocompromised persons and pregnant women). Blood culture and serology (RSAT with confirmatory TAT or AGID) are both used in diagnosis.

q: A shelter dog from rural south Texas is presented with fever, cervical lymphadenopathy, and oral ulcers. The dog lives in an area with known plague activity. Which of the following is most important?
o: Treat empirically with amoxicillin-clavulanate and recheck in 48 hours before deciding on reporting
Collect a lymph node aspirate without PPE for rapid cytology
Isolate the animal, don full PPE including N95 respirator, and report clinical suspicion to the state veterinarian immediately without waiting for lab results
Contact the CDC directly; plague is a human disease that bypasses veterinary reporting channels
e: Cats with suspected plague are a significant zoonotic risk — they can transmit pneumonic plague via respiratory droplets. Full PPE including N95 is required. Plague is immediately reportable on clinical suspicion to the state veterinarian (not solely CDC). Do not perform unprotected procedures or delay reporting pending lab confirmation.

q: Which disinfectant is required to reliably inactivate Leptospira spp. on contaminated shelter surfaces?
o: Leptospires are susceptible to most common disinfectants (bleach, quaternary ammonium, AHP) and to drying; standard cleaning and disinfection protocols are effective
Accelerated hydrogen peroxide (AHP) is the only effective disinfectant
Leptospires are resistant to all common disinfectants; the kennel must be abandoned
Only quaternary ammonium compounds are effective; bleach is inactivated by leptospiral outer membrane proteins
e: Unlike CPV or FPV (which require specifically parvocidal products and prolonged contact times), Leptospira spp. are susceptible to a wide range of common disinfectants and to desiccation. Standard cleaning protocols (organic removal + disinfection) effectively address leptospiral contamination. The main risk is fresh urine on wet surfaces, not prolonged environmental persistence.

q: Q fever (Coxiella burnetii) poses the greatest zoonotic risk to shelter staff in which situation?
o: Administering vaccines to large numbers of cats during a clinic
Processing blood samples from dogs with tick exposure
Cleaning kennels occupied by dogs with respiratory disease
Handling a parturient cat or assisting with delivery of a litter without PPE
e: Coxiella burnetii is shed in extremely high concentrations in birth fluids, placenta, and fetal membranes. Even a single infectious dose can cause Q fever in humans. Parturient animals (particularly cats, cattle, sheep, and goats) are the highest-risk exposure scenario. PPE including gloves and ideally a respirator are essential when assisting with deliveries from animals of unknown Q fever status.

q: Canine influenza virus (CIV) H3N2 was first detected in the US in 2015. Which statement best describes the epidemiological significance of this event?
o: CIV H3N2 is the same strain as equine H3N2, which adapted from horses to dogs, identical to the CIV H3N8 origin story
CIV H3N2 was a re-emergence of the H3N2 strain that had previously circulated in US dogs in the 1990s
CIV H3N2 was a novel introduction from avian/canine influenza circulating in Asia; the US dog population had no prior immunity, leading to rapid spread through shelters and dog facilities
CIV H3N2 is a human-adapted influenza virus that spilled over into dogs
e: CIV H3N2 originated from avian influenza A H3N2 that had adapted to dogs in South Korea and China. It was a completely novel introduction to the US dog population in 2015. Because no prior immunity existed, attack rates in exposed populations were very high. CIV H3N8 — the first identified CIV — originated from equine H3N8; the two strains have different origins.

q: Which of the following best describes SARS-CoV-2 infection in companion animals from a One Health perspective?
o: SARS-CoV-2 is a human-origin pathogen that demonstrated reverse zoonosis (spill-back) into domestic cats, dogs, mink, and wildlife species
SARS-CoV-2 originated in dogs and spilled over to humans — a classic zoonosis
SARS-CoV-2 cannot infect any companion animal species; all reported companion animal cases were due to contaminated swabs
Cats and dogs are the primary reservoir for SARS-CoV-2 and should be routinely tested in shelters
e: SARS-CoV-2 is a human-origin virus (likely originating via a zoonotic spillover event from a bat reservoir via potential intermediate hosts, but established in humans) that then demonstrated reverse zoonosis into companion animals (cats, dogs), captive big cats, mink, ferrets, deer, and other species. Cats are more susceptible than dogs. This is a key example of the bidirectional nature of zoonotic transmission in the One Health framework.

q: Which of the following is the primary methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus causing infections in shelter dogs and cats, distinct from MRSA?
o: Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA)
Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus epidermidis (MRSE)
Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus schleiferi (MRSS)
Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus pseudintermedius (MRSP)
e: MRSP (Staphylococcus pseudintermedius) is the dominant methicillin-resistant staphylococcus in companion animals. It is primarily a veterinary pathogen, though rare human infections occur. MRSA (S. aureus) in pets is usually acquired from human contacts (reverse zoonosis). Knowing the distinction between MRSP and MRSA is a high-yield exam point.

q: A shelter in central California receives a cat from an outdoor colony. The cat has fever, marked cervical lymphadenopathy, and septic shock. A staff member was scratched while handling the cat and did not wear gloves. The shelter is in a county with documented ground squirrel die-offs. What is the priority differential and action?
o: Tularemia; the staff member should be observed for 10 days before PEP is considered

Plague (Yersinia pestis); immediately isolate the cat with full PPE including N95, notify the state veterinarian, and refer the staff member to occupational health / public health for urgent evaluation
Feline infectious peritonitis; no zoonotic risk to the staff member
Cat-scratch disease (Bartonella henselae); staff member needs only routine wound care
e: Ground squirrel die-offs are a plague epizootic indicator in California. Cats in enzootic plague areas are at high risk; they can develop severe septicemic plague and can transmit pneumonic plague to humans via respiratory route. This is an emergency requiring immediate isolation, full PPE, and urgent reporting. The scratched staff member requires urgent medical evaluation for potential plague exposure — do not observe and wait.

q: In an outbreak investigation, what is the purpose of a "case definition"?
o: The number of animals required to constitute an "outbreak" under state law
A dictionary definition of the disease being investigated, used for staff training
A legal definition of which animals the shelter is responsible for under its operating agreement
The minimum clinical, epidemiological, and/or laboratory criteria an animal must meet to be counted as a case in the outbreak
e: A case definition is an epidemiological tool: it specifies the minimum criteria (clinical signs, exposure history, time window, lab confirmation) that an animal must meet to be counted as a case. A well-constructed case definition is sensitive enough not to miss cases but specific enough to exclude unrelated disease, enabling accurate counting and analysis of outbreak scope and pattern.

q: An epidemic curve for a shelter CPV outbreak shows a sharp, narrow single peak with all cases occurring within a 2-day window. What type of outbreak does this suggest?
o: Sentinel surveillance event — the curve shape indicates these are unrelated background cases, not an outbreak
Point source outbreak — all animals were likely exposed to the same source at approximately the same time
Propagated outbreak — cases are spreading from animal to animal over successive generations
Continuous common-source outbreak — an ongoing contamination source is infecting animals over an extended period
e: A sharp, narrow single peak with cases clustered within one incubation period is the classic signature of a point-source outbreak — all cases were exposed to a common source at approximately the same time (e.g., a contaminated intake area, a batch of contaminated supplies, or a single highly infectious animal that all others were exposed to simultaneously). Propagated outbreaks show successive waves; continuous source outbreaks show a plateau.

q: During a shelter respiratory disease outbreak, which of the following flow-management practices is most important to prevent further spread?
o: Sick and healthy animals should be intermingled to accelerate herd immunity development
Staff should work in the healthy population first, then move to the sick or quarantine population, never reversing this direction during a single shift
Staff should work in the sick wards first, then the healthy population, to get the highest-risk work done early in the shift
Staff flow direction is less important than disinfectant concentration, which should be doubled during outbreaks
e: Directional flow from clean (healthy) to dirty (sick) is a fundamental infection-control principle in shelter medicine. Staff who work in the sick population and then enter the healthy population carry pathogens on their hands, clothing, and shoes. This principle applies to housing assignment, staff movement, and supply flow. Reversing direction during a shift is one of the most common outbreak amplification errors in shelters.

q: During a CPV outbreak, the shelter considers emergency vaccination of uninfected dogs in the population. What is the primary rationale and limitation of this intervention?
o: Emergency vaccination is contraindicated during an active outbreak because it will spread the virus via modified-live virus vaccine shedding
Emergency vaccination will immediately protect all vaccinated dogs including those already incubating CPV
Emergency vaccination will reduce spread to susceptible animals not yet exposed but will not protect dogs already incubating infection; the vaccine cannot reverse ongoing infection
Emergency vaccination will eliminate the need for isolation and quarantine measures
e: Emergency vaccination during an outbreak reduces the population of susceptible animals who have not yet been exposed, thereby limiting further spread. However, animals already incubating the pathogen at time of vaccination cannot be "rescued" — the vaccine takes 7–14 days to confer immunity. Vaccination does not eliminate the need for isolation and quarantine of sick and exposed animals. MLV vaccines for CPV do not pose a meaningful shedding risk in a shelter setting that would worsen the outbreak.

q: A state animal health official systematically contacts all shelters in the state weekly during a respiratory disease season to collect case count data. This is an example of which type of surveillance?
o: Sentinel surveillance (passive variant)
Passive surveillance
Syndromic surveillance
Active surveillance
e: Active surveillance involves authorities systematically seeking out case data from defined sources — the opposite of passive surveillance in which reporters submit data only when they identify a case on their own initiative. Contacting all shelters on a regular schedule to collect data is a classic active surveillance design. Syndromic surveillance uses near-real-time aggregate data streams (e.g., electronic health records) without requiring individual case identification.

q: The "iceberg phenomenon" in disease surveillance refers to which concept?
o: Laboratory confirmation is required before any disease appears in surveillance data, hiding the true burden of clinically diagnosed cases
The fact that most disease outbreaks begin in cold climates and spread southward
Surveillance systems capture only recently emerged diseases, missing the long history of established endemic pathogens
Passive surveillance captures only the visible tip of disease burden; the majority of cases are subclinical, mild, or undiagnosed and go unreported
e: The iceberg phenomenon illustrates why passive surveillance consistently underestimates disease burden. Like an iceberg, only the most severe, clinically apparent, diagnosed, and reported cases are "visible above the waterline." The much larger number of mild, subclinical, undiagnosed, or unreported cases remain invisible. Active surveillance studies are used to characterize the full iceberg and estimate true incidence.

q: Which of the following best describes the concept of "biobanking" in the context of shelter disease surveillance?
o: Maintaining a database of adoption records linked to veterinary outcome data
Preserving diagnostic samples (serum, tissue, fecal material) from unexplained deaths and disease clusters for potential retrospective testing when new pathogens are later identified
Storing licensed vaccines at appropriate temperatures to maintain potency
Maintaining a financial reserve to fund diagnostic testing during outbreaks
e: Biobanking involves preserving biological samples from disease events so that, if a new pathogen is later identified or a new diagnostic test becomes available, retrospective testing can determine when the pathogen first appeared in the population. This is a powerful surveillance tool — it was used to identify when SARS-CoV-2 first circulated in various populations by testing archived samples predating the outbreak. Shelters can contribute to this by retaining necropsy samples and serum from unexplained disease clusters.

q: A shelter participates in a regional collaborative that shares anonymous, de-identified aggregate disease data weekly across 12 shelters in the metro area. What is the primary surveillance benefit of this approach?
o: Regional outbreaks that no single shelter would detect alone become detectable when cases are aggregated across multiple facilities
It eliminates the need for passive surveillance reporting to state and federal agencies
It allows the state veterinarian to access individual animal records for auditing purposes
It converts passive surveillance into active surveillance by having shelters report to each other
e: Collaborative data sharing multiplies the epidemiological power of individual shelter data. A disease that produces 2 cases in shelter A and 3 cases in shelter B and 2 in shelter C in the same week might go unnoticed by each shelter individually (each within their normal baseline), but the combined signal of 7 cases in one week across co-located facilities is anomalous and detectable. This is the rationale behind regional surveillance networks.

q: From a One Health perspective, which of the following best describes the role of shelter veterinarians in disease surveillance?
o: Shelter veterinarians should report disease events directly to the CDC, bypassing the state veterinarian
Shelter veterinarians function solely as clinicians; public health surveillance is the responsibility of public health officials, not veterinarians

Shelter veterinarians function simultaneously as clinicians, infection-control officers, mandatory reporters, and surveillance node operators within the One Health framework — integrating animal health, public health, and community engagement
Shelter veterinarians are only obligated to report zoonotic diseases; animal-only diseases do not require reporting
e: This is the central synthesis point of this subdomain. The ABVP exam consistently tests the integrated One Health role of the shelter veterinarian — not just clinical knowledge but the understanding that disease recognition, infection control, mandatory reporting, community communication, and data contribution to surveillance systems are all part of the role. A case scenario presenting a disease cluster will reward candidates who address all four dimensions: diagnose and treat; control spread; report to the right authority; document and preserve data.

q: Which agent did viral metagenomics implicate as most likely responsible for the shelter vomiting outbreak?
o: Rotavirus I
Feline astrovirus
Carnivore bocaparvovirus 3
Norovirus GVI
e: Feline astrovirus was present in all pools at high prevalence and temporally tied to the outbreak.

q: What did testing of asymptomatic control cats housed in the same areas reveal?
o: About 56% were also shedding astrovirus
None were shedding the virus
They cleared infection in 24 hours
All were shedding rotavirus
e: 5 of 9 (56%) clinically unaffected control cats also shed astrovirus, indicating significant asymptomatic shedding.

q: Fecal samples collected ~1 year before and after the outbreak supported which conclusion?
o: The outbreak was caused by panleukopenia
Shedding lasted under 24 hours
Astrovirus is a normal commensal in this shelter
Astrovirus was only temporarily associated with the outbreak
e: No astrovirus was detected before or after, so the virus was temporarily linked to the outbreak rather than commensal.

q: Which species, unlike rabbits, was highly susceptible to SARS-CoV-2 AND transmitted it between conspecifics?
o: Rabbits (Oryctolagus cuniculus)
Raccoon dogs
Egyptian rousettes
White-tailed deer
e: Raccoon dogs were highly susceptible and could transmit between conspecifics, unlike rabbits which did not transmit.

q: What key shortcoming did the authors highlight regarding SARS-CoV-2 in animals?
o: No human cases to compare
Absence of an adequate animal surveillance system to follow viral evolution
Lack of any susceptible species
Overuse of animal vaccines
e: They stress that animal circulation has not been matched by an adequate surveillance system to track viral evolution.

q: Which wild animals were described as potential natural reservoirs of SARS-CoV-2?
o: White-tailed deer, Egyptian rousettes, and minks
Horses and cattle
Salmon and trout
Pigeons and rats
e: White-tailed deer, Egyptian rousettes, and minks were named as potential natural reservoirs.

q: During the 2020–22 highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI) H5 epidemics monitored in the Netherlands, HPAI H5 infection was reported in how many wild bird species?
e: Infection was reported across 51 bird species during the two epidemic seasons.

q: During the 2020–22 highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI) H5 epidemics in the Netherlands, which statement best describes the wild bird species groups with the highest reported mortality?
o: Varied per epidemic year (geese versus sea birds)
Were only raptors
Included no waterfowl
Were identical each year
e: 2020–21 mainly affected Anatidae/barnacle geese; 2021–22 hit sea birds (Sandwich terns and northern gannets).

q: The recommended surveillance approach was to:
o: Monitor live and dead wild birds
Cull all poultry
Stop monitoring wild birds
Vaccinate wild birds
e: Monitoring live and dead wild birds was recommended for tracking HPAI dynamics.

q: The most plausible source of H5N1 infection in mammals was:
o: Contaminated water only
Close contact with or ingestion of infected birds
Mosquito bites
Human handlers
e: Close contact with and ingestion of infected birds was the most plausible source.

q: Compared with previous waves, the current panzootic affected:
o: Only poultry
A larger geographic area and more mammal species
Fewer species and a smaller area
No mammals
e: >48 species across 26 countries, a far larger scope than prior waves.

q: The review warns that H5N1 may be:
o: Adapting to infect mammals, raising pandemic concern
Already eradicated
Permanently limited to birds
Becoming less infectious
e: Mutations and possible mammal-to-mammal transmission suggest adaptation and pandemic risk.

q: How was highly pathogenic avian influenza (H5N1) confirmed in this cat's brain and lung tissue?
o: Blood culture
Serology
Indirect fluorescent antibody
Real-time RT-PCR
e: Influenza A/H5 was confirmed in brain and pulmonary tissues by real-time RT-PCR.

q: A case report documented multisystemic H5N1 highly pathogenic avian influenza in a 4.5-year-old male castrated domestic shorthair cat, confirmed by real-time RT-PCR in both lung and brain tissues. What exposure feature did this case highlight as novel?
o: Extensive outdoor roaming
A predominantly indoor cat with minimal outdoor access
Known contact with an infected cat
Recent vaccination failure
e: Infection occurred in a largely indoor cat with minimal known outdoor access, supporting the possibility of indirect environmental contamination or unrecognized transport hosts and expanding the understood exposure risk for feline H5N1.

q: A 4.5-year-old predominantly indoor domestic shorthair cat presented with lethargy, fever, severe respiratory distress, and neurologic dysfunction confirmed to be H5N1 highly pathogenic avian influenza. Despite aggressive supportive care, what was the outcome?
o: Spontaneous resolution
Full recovery
Humane euthanasia after deterioration
Improvement on antivirals
e: Despite intravenous fluids, antiemetics, and NSAIDs, the cat's condition rapidly deteriorated, necessitating humane euthanasia.
